query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA), accelerated coupled degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature is driven by mechanically assisted, galvanically selective dissolution along the hard/soft interphase network: sliding ruptures thermally softened passive films faster than they can repassivate, exposing adjacent electrochemically dissimilar phases; micro-galvanic currents then preferentially dissolve the anodic phase at and near interphase boundaries, undermining the load-bearing tribolayer, increasing third-body abrasion, and keeping the surface depassivated. This feedback causes total material loss to exceed the sum of wear-only and corrosion-only losses.
generation.material_initial_state: Polished, as-cast multiphase eutectic HEA comprising alternating hard intermetallic-rich lamellae and softer solid-solution lamellae with an electrically continuous interphase boundary network; native passive film formed in air prior to testing.
generation.intervention: Eliminate interphase galvanic couples by solutionizing/homogenizing the same composition to a near-single-phase solid solution (followed by aging or cold work if needed to match bulk hardness within experimental scatter) while keeping composition, grain size scale, counterface, load, and environment constant.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating tribocorrosion at 100 °C in aerated, chloride-bearing aqueous electrolyte at open-circuit potential using an inert counterface (e.g., alumina ball), normal load and sliding kinematics fixed for both microstructures; matched baseline measurements include (i) dry sliding in inert gas at 100 °C and (ii) static immersion corrosion without sliding at 100 °C under otherwise identical electrochemical conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Connectivity and area fraction of the hard/soft interphase boundary network, the galvanic potential difference between phases, and the stability/thickness of the high-temperature passive/tribo-oxide film within the wear track.
generation.mechanism: Sliding contact at elevated temperature repeatedly ruptures the passive/tribo-oxide film at interphase boundaries where hardness and deformation mismatch are highest. Because the adjacent phases have different electrochemical potentials, the harder phase acts relatively cathodic and the softer phase relatively anodic, establishing local galvanic cells that drive selective dissolution of the anodic phase in freshly exposed regions. This interfacial trenching destabilizes the nascent tribolayer, promotes crack initiation and spallation, and generates debris that increases abrasive wear, while the newly exposed surface area sustains higher anodic current; the depassivation–repassivation cycle is thus biased toward dissolution, causing super-additive material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a matched baseline defined by the sum of wear-only (dry, inert) and corrosion-only (static, no sliding) losses, the multiphase eutectic microstructure will show positive synergy (total material loss under simultaneous wear–corrosion greater than additive). Wear volume and friction-induced damage will increase compared to dry sliding, and the time-averaged anodic current (or mass loss) during sliding will exceed the static corrosion case. After homogenization to a near-single-phase state, the super-additive effect will be strongly reduced or approach additivity; selective interfacial trenching will be absent, wear debris chemistry will be less enriched in anodically dissolving constituents, and the corrosion current transient during sliding will be smaller than in the multiphase case. Magnitudes of these changes are expected to be detectable beyond experimental scatter, but precise factors are uncertain without data.
generation.baseline: Additive reference constructed as the sum of (a) wear-only material loss measured by dry sliding in inert gas at 100 °C and (b) corrosion-only mass loss (or equivalent thickness loss) measured during static immersion at 100 °C in the same electrolyte and electrochemical condition for an equal time.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism requires: (1) at least two electrochemically distinct phases in electrical contact; (2) an aqueous or otherwise conductive corrosive environment that supports anodic dissolution; (3) temperatures and contact stresses high enough that passive/tribo-oxide films are periodically ruptured and repassivation cannot keep pace; and (4) an exposed interphase network within the wear track. If the alloy is single-phase, the environment is non-conductive (e.g., oil), repassivation is rapid (lower temperature, benign electrolyte), the surface is held sufficiently cathodic to suppress dissolution, or the interphase network is electrically or mechanically isolated from the contact, the predicted synergy should diminish or disappear.
generation.uncertainty: Which phase is anodic versus cathodic depends on exact composition and environment, and the magnitude of galvanic potentials and repassivation kinetics at 100 °C are unknown here. The relative contributions of third-body abrasion versus film-softening to the total wear are also uncertain. Quantitative effect sizes (e.g., fold-changes in wear rate or current) cannot be predicted without specific data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two specimens from the same EHEA composition: (A) as-cast multiphase eutectic and (B) solutionized/aged to a near-single-phase solid solution with matched bulk hardness within experimental uncertainty. Conduct tribocorrosion tests at 100 °C in aerated chloride solution at open-circuit potential with identical counterface, load, stroke, frequency, and duration. For each specimen, also measure (i) dry sliding wear in inert gas at 100 °C and (ii) static corrosion at 100 °C without sliding for the same time. Compare total material loss under simultaneous wear–corrosion to the additive baseline for each microstructure. Perform post-test cross-sectional microscopy/EDS across wear tracks and analyze debris chemistry.
measurements: Wear track volume (3D profilometry) and corresponding wear rate
In situ current density or charge passed during sliding at OCP (or potentiostatic control) and static immersion
Open-circuit potential transients during sliding and between passes
Cross-sectional SEM/TEM with EDS/EBSD to detect interfacial trenching and selective phase attack
Surface and debris chemistry (XPS/EDS) to identify enrichment of anodically dissolving elements
Coefficient of friction and its evolution with time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if either: (1) the near-single-phase specimen exhibits a similar level of positive synergy as the multiphase eutectic (total material loss under simultaneous wear–corrosion not meaningfully reduced and remaining greater than additive by an amount comparable to the multiphase case) while showing no evidence of preferential interfacial attack, or (2) in the multiphase specimen the total material loss under simultaneous wear–corrosion does not exceed the additive baseline and the sliding current does not exceed the static corrosion current within experimental uncertainty.
